title: Introduce prefetch-fidelity-matrix and cross-model token-churn harness
author: Aisha Patel
description:
Motivation: We need a compact, reproducible harness to evaluate prefetch and KV-cache strategies across heterogeneous model mix workloads and to stress token churn patterns that expose kernel pressure and microburst tail behavior. This PR adds the Prefetch Fidelity Matrix (PFM) runner and the Cross-Model Token-Churn Harness (CMTC) plus a reporting pipeline that emits a kernel-pressure matrix and an occupancy heatmap for per-kernel attribution.

What this contains: - A modular runner that composes: (1) session priming and configurable prefix distributions, (2) an adaptive prefetcher shim that can simulate dead/overfetch and partial-key eviction policies, and (3) a token-churn injector that creates correlated short bursts and long-tail churn with per-session variability. - Telemetry exporters that emit per-step kernel occupancy estimates, async-kernel queue lengths, and a kernel-pressure matrix (CSV + JSONL) compatible with our flamegrid visualizer. - A lightweight evaluator harness that runs baseline and candidate prefetch policies, computes p50/p95/p99 delta matrices, and generates a fidelity score that weighs latency, token-cost, and quality regressions (relative perplexity on synthetic masked prompts). - Config-driven YAML workload descriptors for easy reproduction and a small sample corpus used in internal benchmarks.

Why it's different: Existing runners focus on sequence-mix and steady-state bursts. This harness targets cross-model interference and token-turnover stability: e.g., scenarios where short high-entropy prompts repeatedly evict prefetched KV pages and produce tail amplification on specific kernels. The kernel-pressure matrix maps model-layer/kernel combos to observed tail amplification so teams can prioritize kernel optimizations.

Compatibility & safety: - No production serving changes; runner lives entirely in benchmark-lab and uses existing mock serving interfaces. - Default workloads use conservative resource parameters; a separate opt-in config triggers adversarial churn.

Checklist: - [x] Prefetch shim and eviction policies implemented - [x] Token-churn injector with parameterized distributions - [x] Kernel-pressure exporter and occupancy heatmap generator - [x] YAML workload descriptors and quickstart README - [x] Unit tests for sampling and exporter logic - [x] End-to-end smoke runs in CI with synthetic corpus

How to run (summary): ./benchctl run --workload workloads/pfm/cross_model_churn.yaml --out reports/pfm/round-001 --policy prefetch:conservative

Expected outcomes: The first internal run shows a 12% p95 reduction for the conservative prefetch policy vs no-prefetch on mixed-bert-compat models, but a 4% p99 increase for aggressive prefetch in high-churn configs. Results and artifacts are attached to the PR CI job for quick inspection.

review_thread: Marco Li: Looks solid overall — can you clarify how occupancy_est is computed? We should avoid heavy probes in CI runs.
Aisha Patel: occupancy_est is a heuristic derived from token footprint and inferred CUDA occupancy; added comments and a unit test to ensure it runs quickly in CI.
Daniel Kim: The YAML descriptors are convenient. Can we add a stress variant that runs fewer sessions but higher churn for quickdog runs?
Aisha Patel: Added workloads/pfm/cross_model_churn_quick.yaml and updated bench-smoke CI to run it.
Priya Rao: I saw the p99 regression in aggressive prefetch config. Can we add an automated check that flags >3% p99 regressions compared to baseline?
Aisha Patel: Added delta thresholds to fidelity_score.py; CI will annotate artifacts when regression exceeds threshold.
release_notes: Add Prefetch Fidelity Matrix runner and Cross-Model Token-Churn harness. New reporting artifacts: kernel-pressure matrix and occupancy heatmap. Useful for prioritizing kernel-level optimizations and prefetch policy tuning.
notes: This PR is intended for internal benchmark-lab usage only. The next follow-up will add a scheduler-aware variant that exercises node-local contention and GPU oversubscription scenarios.
